clue.text: Tom behaving like an ape ?

indicators.note: behaving like something places that description in front of the tom, so its piece leads

parts.note: to ape is to imitate, so ape-like behaviour is to copy
a tom is a male cat

explanation.surface: A tomcat is seen mimicking the antics of an ape.
explanation.definitionFit: An imitator who slavishly follows others is a copier, the very thing the clue describes a tom doing.

clue.text: Shrinks from business arrangements

definitions.meaning: deals and binding agreements in commerce

explanation.surface: Something gets smaller after business deals.
explanation.definitionFit: To contract is to shrink, and contracts are also legal agreements.

clue.text: No stamp might upset him

indicators.note: upset suggests knocking the letters of no stamp into a new order

explanation.surface: A letter carrier is annoyed by an unstamped envelope.
explanation.definitionFit: A mail carrier would be troubled by an unstamped letter, since he must collect the postage due.

clue.text: One whose work is of a fitting character

definitions.text: One whose work is of a fitting character

parts.words: One whose work is of a fitting character
parts.note: fitting reads as tailoring, and character as a role in a play, so this is someone who dresses actors

explanation.surface: Someone does suitable, appropriate work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fitting' looks like 'suitable', but it is a fitting of clothes on a stage character.
explanation.definitionFit: A costumier makes or supplies outfits for theatrical roles.

clue.text: Roundabout way to spot winners ?

indicators.note: roundabout says the word spot is turned around and read backwards

explanation.surface: A tipster's indirect method of picking winners.
explanation.definitionFit: The tops are the best, the ones who come out ahead.

clue.text: Bare skin prominent in this American city

definitions.text: Bare skin prominent in this American city

parts.words: Bare skin prominent in this American city
parts.note: being in the buff means naked, and that word stands prominently at the front of the city's name

explanation.surface: Nudity is on open display in some American city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In the buff' means naked; BUFF is prominent, at the very front, of this city in New York State.
explanation.definitionFit: The clue points to a New York State city whose name begins with a word for naked skin.

clue.text: Not to be seen in Cork — on the contrary

definitions.text: Not to be seen in Cork — on the contrary

parts.words: Not to be seen in Cork — on the contrary
parts.note: the Irish city misleads: reversing the statement, a cork is seen in this narrow part of a container

explanation.surface: Something is absent from the Irish city of Cork.
explanation.walkthrough: Cork looks like the Irish city; reverse the statement and a cork is found in this narrow top of a wine container.
explanation.definitionFit: The narrow neck of a wine container holds the cork; the word also means a congestion point.

clue.text: The whole beastly family

parts.note: beastly sounds like nasty but means made up of beasts, so this is every animal of a region

explanation.surface: An entire horrid household.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Beastly family' sounds like dreadful relations, but it is all the animals together.
explanation.definitionFit: Fauna is the animal life of a region taken as a whole.

clue.text: The loan of a place in Eire

indicators.note: of here says the place is made from the letters of the loan, rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone borrows a property in Ireland.
explanation.walkthrough: The setter gives the anagram with only 'of' to signal it: THE LOAN rearranged is a town on the Shannon.
explanation.definitionFit: Athlone is a town on the River Shannon in the Irish midlands.

clue.text: Weight one put on at the seaside ?

indicators.note: put on means the second piece is attached after the first

parts.note: oz is the abbreviation for ounce, a weight
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone gains weight on a beach holiday.
explanation.walkthrough: Ozone was the popular name for the bracing sea air at a British resort.
explanation.definitionFit: Ozone is the old popular term for fresh, bracing sea air.

clue.text: Built in Cleopatra's sails

parts.note: a line from Shakespeare's Antony and Cleopatra: swallows have built their homes in the queen's sails, an ill omen

explanation.surface: Something was constructed in the rigging of the Egyptian queen's ship.
explanation.walkthrough: The source is Antony and Cleopatra, Act IV: 'Swallows have built / In Cleopatra's sails their nests.'
explanation.definitionFit: The quotation completes with the birds' homes, which is what swallows built in the sails.

clue.text: His wife was, by definition, something of a mouse !

definitions.text: His wife was, by definition, something of a mouse !

parts.words: His wife was, by definition, something of a mouse !
parts.note: the hero of The Taming of the Shrew married Katharina, and a shrew is a small mouse-like animal

explanation.surface: A man's wife was meek and timid, a proper mouse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mouse' suggests a timid woman, but the play is The Taming of the Shrew, and a shrew is a mouse-like creature; its hero is Katharina's husband.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's suitor in The Taming of the Shrew weds Katharina, the shrew of the title.

clue.text: Strange matter to create a disturbance

parts.note: rum is old British slang for odd or strange
pus is the matter from an infected wound

explanation.surface: Some odd substance causes an upset.
explanation.definitionFit: A rumpus is a noisy commotion, an uproar.

clue.text: "—— on Airly Beacon, With his baby on my knee!" (Kingsley)

definitions.text: on Airly Beacon, With his baby on my knee!

parts.words: on Airly Beacon, With his baby on my knee!
parts.note: the closing stanza of Charles Kingsley's poem Airly Beacon, where the deserted girl is left by herself with her child

explanation.surface: A line of Victorian verse about a girl on a hill holding her baby.
explanation.walkthrough: Kingsley's poem Airly Beacon ends 'Oh the weary haunt for me, / All alone on Airly Beacon, / With his baby on my knee!'
explanation.definitionFit: The missing words of the quotation describe the abandoned girl being solitary, by herself.

clue.text: A word of deep significance

parts.note: read literally, a word whose meaning is depth

explanation.surface: Some utterance carries weighty meaning.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Deep significance' suggests a meaningful word; it is a word that signifies deepness.
explanation.definitionFit: Profundity means depth, of water or of thought.

clue.text: Shelley's tragic family

parts.note: Percy Bysshe Shelley wrote a verse tragedy about a Roman noble family of the sixteenth century

explanation.surface: A poet's relatives met a sad end.
explanation.definitionFit: Shelley's verse drama The Cenci tells of Beatrice and her tyrannical father, a Roman noble household.

clue.text: Sounds as if drink flowed freely — lowering of the King's resistance here ?

definitions.text: lowering of the King's resistance here ?

indicators.note: the clue says the place's name is heard as the following phrase

parts.note: mead is an old drink of honey, and runny means flowing freely

explanation.surface: Drink was flowing freely when a king was finally made to give in.
explanation.walkthrough: King John's resistance to the barons was lowered at RUNNYMEDE, a meadow by the Thames, where he sealed Magna Carta in 1215.
explanation.definitionFit: The Thames-side meadow is where King John yielded to his barons and sealed Magna Carta.

clue.text: Gone rusty, but not through age

definitions.text: Gone rusty, but not through age

indicators.note: rust is decay, so the letters of gone rusty have decayed into a new order, though not from age

explanation.surface: Someone has lost their touch, though not from getting old.
explanation.definitionFit: A juvenile could hardly have rusted through age, being young.

clue.text: They set out to make an artistic impression

definitions.text: They set out to make an artistic impression

parts.words: They set out to make an artistic impression
parts.note: an impression here is a print taken from an incised plate, which these craftsmen cut

explanation.surface: Some people try to impress others with their creativity.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Make an impression' sounds like impressing people, but it is a print pulled from a cut plate.
explanation.definitionFit: Engravers incise designs on plates from which artistic prints are taken.

clue.text: This one'll make you sweat !

parts.note: read literally: a drug or treatment whose purpose is to bring on perspiration

explanation.surface: A warning that some task will be hard work.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests an ordeal, but the clue is literal: a medicine that causes sweating.
explanation.definitionFit: A sudorific is a medicine that induces perspiration, a diaphoretic.

clue.text: A sound measure

parts.note: sound looks like sensible but is noise, so this is a unit for loudness

explanation.surface: A sensible step.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sound measure' suggests a sensible step; it is a unit of loudness.
explanation.definitionFit: The decibel is the unit for measuring the intensity of noise.

clue.text: Ho! this is calculated to put you in your place

definitions.text: Ho! this is calculated to put you in your place

parts.words: Ho! this is calculated to put you in your place
parts.note: put the word for calculating after HO and you get accommodation, which puts you in your home

explanation.surface: A shout prefaces a remark meant to cut someone down to size.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put you in your place' sounds like a snub, but it means giving you a home: HO followed by this word means accommodation, and the word itself means calculating.
explanation.definitionFit: Using means calculating or employing, and joined after HO it makes a word for dwellings.

clue.text: It is generally closed when nearly all the strikers are out

definitions.text: It is generally closed when nearly all the strikers are out

parts.words: It is generally closed when nearly all the strikers are out
parts.note: strikers suggests workers on strike, but they are batsmen; in cricket a side's turn at bat is often declared closed before all are out

explanation.surface: A business shuts down when most of its workforce walks out.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket a team's turn to bat ends when ten of its eleven batsmen, the strikers, are out, or the captain declares it closed.
explanation.definitionFit: An innings in cricket is a side's turn at batting, ended when nearly all its batsmen are dismissed.

clue.text: Ten years and 'more on the downward path

definitions.text: Ten years and 'more on the downward path

parts.words: Ten years and 'more on the downward path
parts.note: a span of ten years with a little more on the end gives a word for being in moral decline

explanation.surface: Someone has spent over a decade going downhill.
explanation.walkthrough: Ten years is a DECADE; a little more, NT, makes a word for one in decline.
explanation.definitionFit: Decadent means in moral or cultural decline, sliding downhill.

clue.text: A beetle on the watch

parts.note: put this word on the front of watch and you get the name of a wood-boring beetle

explanation.surface: An insect crawls over a timepiece.
explanation.walkthrough: The deathwatch beetle bores into old timber; its ticking was once thought to foretell a death.
explanation.definitionFit: Placed before watch, the word names the deathwatch, a wood-boring beetle.

clue.text: Father takes in an engineer with much apprehension

indicators.note: takes in means the first piece encloses the second

parts.note: dad is an everyday word for father
RE stands for the Royal Engineers, a British army corps

explanation.surface: A father welcomes an engineer, though nervously.
explanation.definitionFit: Dread is great fear or apprehension.

clue.text: Country in which a man is soundly accused of being foolish ?

indicators.note: the clue asks for the accusation as it sounds when spoken

parts.note: a man called a silly goose would be told 'you gander!', a gander being a male goose

explanation.surface: In some nation a man is roundly abused for his stupidity.
explanation.walkthrough: A gander is a male goose and 'goose' means a fool, so the man is told 'You gander!'
explanation.definitionFit: Uganda is an East African nation.

clue.text: "Don't do it, lady" begged the old Kentucky émigré

definitions.text: "Don't do it, lady" begged the old Kentucky émigré

parts.words: "Don't do it, lady" begged the old Kentucky émigré
parts.note: Stephen Foster's song My Old Kentucky Home has the singer far from home telling his lady not to cry any more

explanation.surface: An exile from Kentucky pleads with a woman not to do something.
explanation.walkthrough: The chorus of My Old Kentucky Home begins 'Weep no more, my lady'.
explanation.definitionFit: The song asks the lady to stop crying, so 'don't do it' refers to shedding tears.

clue.text: Team of walkers in the Lake District ?

definitions.text: Team of walkers in the Lake District ?

parts.words: Team of walkers in the Lake District ?
parts.note: a side is a team, and walkers amble, so a side of amblers names a Cumbrian town

explanation.surface: A group of hikers is out on the fells of north-west England.
explanation.walkthrough: AMBLE (walk) + SIDE (team) is a town at the head of Windermere in the Lake District, a hill-walking region of north-west England.
explanation.definitionFit: Ambleside is a town at the northern end of Windermere, in Cumbria's lake country.

clue.text: Not much colour in hunting equipment

indicators.note: in tells the solver the letters sit inside the words hunting equipment

explanation.surface: Hunting gear is drab and muted.
explanation.definitionFit: A tinge is a slight trace of a hue.

clue.text: "Butcher'd to make a Roman" (Byron)

parts.note: Byron's Childe Harold describes a dying gladiator slaughtered for the crowd's entertainment

explanation.surface: A line of Byron on a gladiator killed for sport.
explanation.walkthrough: Childe Harold's Pilgrimage, Canto IV: 'Butcher'd to make a Roman holiday'.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing word completes Byron's line about a Roman festival day of games.

clue.text: The last people to indulge in slanging matches?

definitions.text: The last people to indulge in slanging matches?

parts.words: The last people to indulge in slanging matches?
parts.note: slanging matches look like quarrels, but read as contests in using slang, which sticklers for correct usage would avoid

explanation.surface: Some folk would never join a shouting match.
explanation.walkthrough: A slanging match is a bout of abuse, but here it means a contest in slang, shunned by sticklers for proper English.
explanation.definitionFit: Purists insist on correct traditional usage and would shun slang.
